titulo_es: Style nuances: synonyms, irony and understatement
descripcion_es: Synonyms with nuances, connotation, euphemism, irony and understatement.
resumen: At the highest level, connotation matters: two synonyms can be praise or criticism (frugal / stingy). This card practises the nuances of near-synonyms, euphemisms and the ironic understatement typical of British English.

explicacion.texto: Many pairs of words describe the same thing with opposite evaluations. Choosing one or the other means taking sides: a politician who is “firm” to his supporters is “stubborn” to his rivals. The educated speaker controls that charge.

filas: careful with money / unwilling to spend (es: ahorrador / tacaño)
firm in purpose / unwilling to change (es: decidido / terco)
sure of oneself / full of oneself (es: seguro de sí / arrogante)
thin in a pleasing way / too thin (es: delgado / flacucho)
eager to know / too interested in others (es: curioso / cotilla)
confident and direct / overbearing (es: asertivo / avasallador)
not conventional / strange (es: poco convencional / raro)
open and honest / rudely direct (es: franco / brusco)
It was not exactly a success.
slightly, a little bit (es: algo, un pelín)
The speech was a tad too long.
politely respectful (announces a criticism) (es: con el debido respeto)
With all due respect, that is nonsense.
to be economical with the truth
not telling the whole truth (euphemism for lying)
The minister was economical with the truth.
We had to let fifty people go.
He's between jobs at the moment.
Her grandfather passed away last year.
irony: not exactly the most… (es: no precisamente el más…)
It was hardly the most exciting match.
I'm not at all convinced (British understatement)
I'm not entirely convinced by the plan.

items: British understatement: “That's a bit unfortunate” can mean “it's a disaster”.
“Quite” is ambiguous: “quite good” (British) usually means “fairly good, nothing more”; “quite brilliant” means “absolutely brilliant”.
“Hardly” is negative: “He hardly works” = he barely works, not “he works hard”.

ejemplos.frase: My grandmother was frugal, not stingy: she just hated waste.
ejemplos.traduccion: Mi abuela era ahorradora, no tacaña: simplemente detestaba el despilfarro.

ejemplos.frase: Our new neighbour is a bit nosy; she always asks where we're going.
ejemplos.traduccion: La nueva vecina es un poco cotilla; siempre pregunta adónde vamos.

ejemplos.frase: The company announced that it would let 300 employees go.
ejemplos.traduccion: La empresa anunció que prescindiría de 300 empleados.

ejemplos.frase: Losing 5–0 at home was not exactly ideal.
ejemplos.traduccion: Perder 5 a 0 en casa no fue precisamente lo ideal.

ejemplos.frase: With all due respect, minister, you have not answered the question.
ejemplos.traduccion: Con el debido respeto, ministro, no ha respondido a la pregunta.

ejemplos.frase: She gave a frank assessment of the team's weaknesses.
ejemplos.traduccion: Hizo una valoración franca de los puntos débiles del equipo.

errores_hispanohablantes.nota: “Hard” is the adverb meaning “with effort” (es: duro); “hardly” means “barely” (es: apenas).

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Thank you for your frank criticism; you're so blunt!
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Thank you for your frank criticism; you're so honest!
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: “Blunt” has a negative connotation (rudely direct); it does not work as praise.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: My boss is very economic with the truth.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: My boss is very economical with the truth.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: The fixed expression is “economical with the truth”.

ejercicios.enunciado: Choose the adjective with a positive connotation.
ejercicios.frase: She's very ___ with money and has saved enough to buy a flat.
ejercicios.explicacion: The first table in Rules and key points contrasts frugal / thrifty (positive connotation: careful with money) with stingy / mean (negative: unwilling to spend). The clue is the favourable outcome in the sentence: thanks to the way he manages his money he has been able to buy a flat, so the adjective must judge saving positively. Thrifty means “careful with money, not wasteful”, with no criticism at all; the other options describe the same behaviour as a fault.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Thrifty” praises saving; the others criticise meanness.
ejercicios.traduccion: Es muy ahorradora y ha conseguido ahorrar lo suficiente para comprarse un piso.

por_opcion.thrifty: Correct: thrifty means “careful with money” (es: ahorrador), praise for good money management.
por_opcion.stingy: Incorrect: stingy means “unwilling to spend” (es: tacaño, rácano), a criticism; it would fit in “he's too stingy to buy anyone a drink”.
por_opcion.mean: Incorrect: in British English mean with money means “stingy” (and in general mean is “petty, unkind”); it criticises, it does not praise.
por_opcion.tight-fisted: Incorrect: tight-fisted means “very stingy” (es: agarrado), informal and pejorative.

glosario.definicion_l: careful and diligent in the use of resources · mindful of the future in spending money
having a surface without slope, tilt in which no part is higher or lower than another · having a relatively broad surface in relation to depth or thickness

ejercicios.enunciado: Choose the adjective with a negative connotation.
ejercicios.frase: He refused to change his mind even when he was clearly wrong; he's so ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table in the card contrasts determined / resolute (firm in purpose, positive) with stubborn / obstinate (unwilling to change, negative). The clue is in the context: “even when he was clearly wrong” turns firmness into a fault, and the exclamation “he's so…” expresses irritation. Stubborn is the critical adjective; the others would describe the same perseverance as a virtue.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The context is critical: “stubborn” = unwilling to change (es: terco).
ejercicios.traduccion: Se negó a cambiar de opinión incluso cuando estaba claro que se equivocaba; es tan terco...

por_opcion.stubborn: Correct: stubborn means “obstinate, pig-headed” (es: terco, cabezota), the critical version of firmness.
por_opcion.determined: Incorrect: determined means “firm in purpose”, a compliment; it would fit if his firmness had a good result.
por_opcion.resolute: Incorrect: resolute means “firm, determined”, positive and rather formal.
por_opcion.committed: Incorrect: committed means “dedicated” (to a cause); it is also positive and does not refer to refusing to change your mind.

glosario.definicion_l: tenaciously unwilling or marked by tenacious unwillingness to yield · not responding to treatment
perform an act, usually with a negative connotation · make a set of changes permanent

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete the euphemism (to die), in the past.
ejercicios.frase: I'm sorry to hear that your father passed ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: The second table in the card includes passed away as a euphemism for “died”. The clue is the condolence formula “I'm sorry to hear that…”, where saying died would be correct but blunter. Pass away is a phrasal verb: the particle away is what gives the sense of “leaving, dying”; without it, pass means “to go past”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Siento mucho lo de tu padre (lamento saber que tu padre ha fallecido).

errores_previstos.explicacion: Pass out means “to faint” or, in some contexts, “to graduate”; not “to die”.
Pass by means “to go past, to go near”; it has no sense of death.
Pass off means “to present something as something else” or “to take place”; the euphemism is pass away.

ejercicios.frase: She works hardly to support her family.
respuestas: She works hard to support her family.
ejercicios.explicacion: The list in the card warns that hardly is negative: it means “barely”, not “with effort”. The clue is the meaning of the sentence: working to support the family implies effort, so the right adverb is hard, which has the same form as the adjective. “She works hardly” would, if anything, say the opposite of what is intended and is also an odd collocation (you would say “she hardly works”, she barely works).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Hardly” = barely; the adverb of effort is “hard”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Trabaja duro para mantener a su familia.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She works hardly to support her family.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: hardly means “barely”; the adverb of effort is hard.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She works hardy to support her family.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Hardy is an adjective (“tough, robust”, a hardy plant), not an adverb of manner.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She hardly works to support her family.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Now the sentence is grammatical, but it says she barely works, the opposite of the intended meaning; you need hard.

glosario.definicion_l: only a very short time before · almost not

ejercicios.enunciado: Choose the option that expresses a softened criticism.
ejercicios.frase: The hotel was ___ the cleanest place I've ever stayed in.
ejercicios.explicacion: The second table includes not exactly as understatement: “not completely”, which often means “not at all”. The clue is the instruction (softened criticism) and the superlative the cleanest: by negating it with not exactly, the speaker implies that the hotel was rather dirty without saying so openly. This is the irony typical of British understatement; the other options intensify the praise instead of softening a criticism.
ejercicios.traduccion: El hotel no era precisamente el sitio más limpio en el que me he alojado.

por_opcion.not exactly: Correct: not exactly negates the superlative ironically and expresses a softened criticism.
por_opcion.absolutely: Incorrect: absolutely the cleanest reinforces the superlative; it would be unqualified praise.
por_opcion.by far: Incorrect: by far the cleanest means “much cleaner than all the others”, emphatic praise.
por_opcion.definitely: Incorrect: definitely the cleanest states with certainty that it was the cleanest; it neither softens nor criticises.

glosario.definicion_l: by a considerable margin

ejercicios.frase: The spokesman was clearly being economical with the ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: The second table in the card includes to be economical with the truth: not telling the whole truth, an educated euphemism for lying or hiding information. The clue is the adjective economical (saving) followed by with the, which forms the fixed expression. It is used above all about politicians and spokespeople, with an ironic tone.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Economical with the truth” = not telling the whole truth.
ejercicios.traduccion: Estaba claro que el portavoz no estaba diciendo toda la verdad.

errores_previstos.explicacion: True is an adjective; after the you need the noun truth.
Verity exists but is very formal and is not part of the fixed expression, which is economical with the truth.
It is understandable, but it breaks the fixed expression; the established euphemism is economical with the truth.

glosario.palabra: to be economical with the truth
glosario.significado: no decir toda la verdad (eufemismo de mentir)

glosario.definicion_l: a male spokesperson

ejercicios.enunciado: Choose the adjective with a negative connotation.
ejercicios.frase: I don't like our new neighbour: she's always asking ___ questions about our private life.
ejercicios.explicacion: The first table contrasts inquisitive / curious (eager to know, neutral or positive) with nosy / prying (too interested in others, negative). The clue is the initial judgement “I don't like our new neighbour” and the subject of the questions, private life: curiosity is presented as intrusion. Nosy means “prying, meddling” (es: cotilla, entrometido) and is the only adjective that expresses that criticism.
ejercicios.traduccion: No me cae bien nuestra nueva vecina: siempre hace preguntas indiscretas sobre nuestra vida privada.

por_opcion.nosy: Correct: nosy means “prying, meddling” (es: cotilla, entrometido); it criticises interest in other people's business.
por_opcion.curious: Incorrect: curious is neutral; it does not express the annoyance conveyed by the sentence.
por_opcion.inquisitive: Incorrect: inquisitive means “eager to learn”, rather positive (an inquisitive child).
por_opcion.interested: Incorrect: interested describes the person, not the questions; “interested questions” is not a natural combination.

glosario.definicion_l: offensively curious or inquisitive
showing curiosity · inquiring or appearing to inquire
a person who lives (or is located) near another · a nearby object of the same kind

ejercicios.frase: Due to the crisis, we will have to let some staff ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: The second table includes to let someone go as a euphemism for “to dismiss”. The clue is the structure let + object (some staff) + gap: the verb let is followed by the infinitive without to, and the fixed expression is let go. It is the usual form in company announcements, because it sounds less harsh than fire or dismiss.
ejercicios.traduccion: Debido a la crisis, tendremos que despedir a parte de la plantilla.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Let out means “to allow to leave” or “to release”; it does not mean to dismiss.
Let is followed by the infinitive without to: let some staff go.
Let down means “to disappoint, to fail someone”; it is not the euphemism for dismissing.

glosario.definicion_l: personnel who assist their superior in carrying out an assigned task · a strong rod or stick with a specialized utilitarian purpose

ejercicios.frase: With all ___ respect, I think your figures are wrong.
ejercicios.explicacion: The second table includes with all due respect as a fixed formula that, paradoxically, announces a criticism or disagreement. The clue is what follows the comma: “I think your figures are wrong”. Due means “owed, deserved” here, and the expression does not allow any other determiner. It is very useful in meetings and debates, although it is worth knowing that it often precedes a sharp objection.
ejercicios.traduccion: Con el debido respeto, creo que sus cifras son erróneas.

por_opcion.due: Correct: with all due respect is the fixed formula (es: con el debido respeto).
por_opcion.my: Incorrect: with all my respect is a calque from Spanish; the English formula has due.
por_opcion.the: Incorrect: “with all the respect” is not the formula; it sounds like a literal translation.
por_opcion.full: Incorrect: full respect exists in other contexts (I have full respect for him), but not in this formula.

glosario.significado: con el debido respeto (anuncia una crítica)

glosario.definicion_l: a diagram or picture illustrating textual material · alternative names for the body of a human being

ejercicios.frase: As a manager, she is ___: she says what she wants without being rude.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table in the card contrasts assertive (positive: confident and direct) with pushy / aggressive (negative: overbearing). The clue is the definition after the colon: “says what she wants without being rude”, that is, firmness without aggression, which is exactly the complimentary sense of assertive. Bossy and aggressive describe the same firmness as a fault.
ejercicios.traduccion: Como directiva, es asertiva: dice lo que quiere sin ser grosera.

por_opcion.assertive: Correct: assertive means “confident, standing up for yourself” without aggression; it is a compliment.
por_opcion.pushy: Incorrect: pushy means “overbearing, too insistent”, with a negative connotation.
por_opcion.bossy: Incorrect: bossy means “always telling others what to do” (es: mandón), critical; it does not fit with “without being rude”.
por_opcion.aggressive: Incorrect: aggressive contradicts “without being rude”. In marketing, aggressive can be complimentary (an aggressive strategy), but not when applied to personal manner.

glosario.definicion_l: aggressively self-assured
marked by aggressive ambition and energy and initiative
offensively self-assured or given to exercising usually unwarranted power
socially incorrect in behavior · (of persons) lacking in refinement or grace

ejercicios.frase: The minister was rather economic with the truth.
respuestas: The minister was rather economical with the truth.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the fixed expression from the second table, to be economical with the truth, and the mistake mentioned in the card: confusing economical with economic. Economic means “relating to the economy” (economic policy), whereas economical means “saving money, cheap to run” (an economical car). Only economical forms the euphemism.
ejercicios.traduccion: El ministro fue bastante parco con la verdad (no contó toda la verdad).

errores_previstos.respuesta: The minister was rather economic with the truth.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: economic means “relating to the economy”; the fixed expression has economical.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The minister was rather economics with the truth.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Economics is the noun (“the science of economics”); you need the adjective economical.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The minister was rather economical with truth.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The fixed expression has an article: economical with the truth.

glosario.definicion_l: using the minimum of time or resources necessary for effectiveness · of or relating to an economy, the system of production and management of material wealth
of or relating to an economy, the system of production and management of material wealth · of or relating to the science of economics
on the contrary · to some (great or small) extent

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with an adverb of irony (not exactly).
ejercicios.frase: It was ___ the most exciting match of the season: nobody scored.
ejercicios.explicacion: The second table includes “Hardly the most…” as irony: not exactly the most… The clue is the explanation after the colon (nobody scored), which reveals that the match was boring. Hardly negates the superlative with an ironic tone, which is what the instruction asks for.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Hardly the most…” = not exactly the most…
ejercicios.traduccion: No fue precisamente el partido más emocionante de la temporada: nadie marcó.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Hard means “difficult, with effort”; the ironic negative word is hardly.
Nearly the most exciting would mean “almost the most exciting”, praise that contradicts nobody scored.
No cannot negate a phrase with the; you would say not the most or hardly the most.
Not the most exciting is grammatical, but it negates in a direct, neutral way; the instruction asks for the ironic adverb, hardly.

glosario.definicion_l: only a very short time before · almost not

ejercicios.enunciado: Choose the neutral or positive adjective.
ejercicios.explicacion: The first table contrasts slim / slender (thin, positive) with skinny / scrawny (too thin, negative). The clue is the instruction, which asks for a neutral or positive adjective, and the context: the description of a model, together with tall, is complimentary. Slender conveys elegance and graceful thinness; the other adjectives suggest excessive or unattractive thinness.
ejercicios.traduccion: La modelo es alta y esbelta.

por_opcion.slender: Correct: slender means “gracefully thin” (es: esbelto), a compliment.
por_opcion.skinny: Incorrect: skinny means “very thin”, somewhat disparaging, although it is used in fashion for clothes (skinny jeans).
por_opcion.scrawny: Incorrect: scrawny means “thin and weak-looking” (es: escuálido, esmirriado), clearly negative.
por_opcion.bony: Incorrect: bony means “so thin that the bones show”; it is disparaging when applied to people.

glosario.definicion_l: being very thin · composed of or containing bone

ejercicios.frase: The soup is a ___ too salty, but otherwise delicious.
ejercicios.explicacion: The second table includes somewhat / a tad / a touch as softeners: “slightly, a little bit”. The clue is the structure “a ___ too salty” followed by a positive judgement (but otherwise delicious): the criticism is softened. A tad and a touch are the forms practised in the card; a bit and a little are also correct and more neutral, so they are accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “A tad / a touch” = a little bit.
ejercicios.traduccion: La sopa está un pelín salada de más, pero por lo demás está deliciosa.

errores_previstos.explicacion: A few goes with plural countable nouns (a few problems); it does not modify adjectives like too salty.
A lot too salty is not natural (you would say far too or much too) and it also intensifies instead of softening.
A pinch is a tiny amount of an ingredient (a pinch of salt); it does not modify adjectives.

glosario.definicion_l: other than as supposed or expected · in other respects or ways

respuestas: I'm not entirely convinced by the argument
ejercicios.explicacion: The second table includes “I'm not entirely convinced” as British understatement: literally “not completely convinced”, but in practice it usually expresses clear disagreement. The order is subject with verb (I'm), not, the adverb entirely before the participle-adjective convinced, and the preposition by with its complement (the argument).
ejercicios.traduccion: No me acaba de convencer el argumento.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I'm entirely not convinced by the argument
errores_previstos.explicacion: Not must come before entirely; “entirely not” negates completely and sounds unnatural.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I'm not convinced entirely by the argument
errores_previstos.explicacion: The degree adverb entirely goes before convinced, not after it.

glosario.significado: no del todo convencido (a menudo, nada convencido)

descripcion_larga_es: At C2 level it is no longer enough to choose a correct word: you have to choose the one that conveys the right evaluation. This card practises near-synonyms with opposite connotations (thrifty versus stingy), euphemisms (let someone go, pass away) and British ironic understatement (not exactly, hardly). Mastering them avoids giving offence unintentionally and lets you understand what the other person is saying between the lines.

contexto.que_es: It is control of connotation: the positive or negative evaluative charge that accompanies the meaning of a word. It includes pairs of near-synonyms with opposite evaluations, euphemisms that soften uncomfortable realities (dismissals, death, lies) and devices of understatement and irony, very characteristic of British English, that say less than one thinks.
contexto.por_que_importa: Choosing the wrong synonym can turn praise into an insult (calling someone blunt when you want to thank them for their frankness) or make a criticism sound much harsher than intended. Moreover, someone who does not recognise British understatement misreads messages: “I'm not entirely convinced” is usually a clear rejection. In diplomacy and in a high-level oral exam, this subtlety is what distinguishes the educated speaker.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: It appears when describing people, assessing proposals or reports, giving bad news and disagreeing politely in a meeting. The signals are the tone of the context (praise or criticism) and fixed formulas such as with all due respect, which announces an objection. Spanish speakers tend to translate literally and directly; educated English prefers euphemism and understatement, and there are also misleading look-alikes such as hardly, which does not mean “hard” (es: duramente).
